explanations.answer: Only as long as he lives
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). Once the man has died, that authority is finished. Paul is talking to people who know the law, so I think he trusts them to see where he's headed.

explanations.answer: Only as long as he obeys it
explanations.explanation: Close to how we'd think about it, friend, but Paul never makes obedience the clock. He says the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). Staying in line doesn't switch it off, and slipping up doesn't either. Life is the measure here, not how well somebody did.

explanations.answer: Only as long as he remembers it
explanations.explanation: If forgetting set you free, I'd have been released from half my own recipes years ago! But Paul doesn't tie it to memory at all. He says the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). Remembering or forgetting doesn't change that.

Careful, baker, this one flips what Paul says. In his picture, if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage (Romans 7:2). The binding lasts only while the husband lives. After that, she isn't held by it anymore.

Right, because Paul says the opposite. A married woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies, she is released from the law of marriage (Romans 7:2). The husband's death is what ends the binding. Paul sets up this picture so he can show something bigger in a few verses.

That's the word Paul uses, baker. If she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress (Romans 7:3). The timing is the whole point. Same woman, same new husband, but everything depends on whether the first husband is still living.

Nothing in Paul's picture is about where she's from, friend. He says she's called an adulteress if she's joined to another man while her husband is still alive (Romans 7:3). The question is only whether the husband is living. Her homeland never comes up.

I can see why that sounds right, but it's not Paul's word. He says she is called an adulteress if she's joined to another man while her husband is still alive (Romans 7:3). He names the act and leaves it there. He doesn't say what else anyone would call her.

explanations.answer: Him who was raised from the dead
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says they died to the law through the body of Christ, that they might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead (Romans 7:4). Remember the widow in the picture, who is free to belong to someone new. Paul is telling his brothers they have that same kind of freedom, and it leads to Christ.

explanations.answer: Moses who gave them the law
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, is the one who stands for the law, so I get the pick. But Paul says they died to the law so that they might belong to Him who was raised from the dead (Romans 7:4). That's Christ, not Moses. The new belonging is to a risen person.

explanations.answer: Abraham the father of us all
explanations.explanation: Abraham is called the father of us all in Romans 4:16, so he's a fair guess. But in this verse Paul says they died to the law that they might belong to Him who was raised from the dead (Romans 7:4). Abraham wasn't raised from the dead. Paul is pointing to Christ.
That's it, friend. Paul says they belong to the risen Christ in order that we might bear fruit to God (Romans 7:4). Notice he says "we," so he's counting himself in. The fruit goes to God.
Rome is where the believers live, so I see how it slid in. But Paul says the fruit is borne to God (Romans 7:4). Rome is the address on the letter. God is who the fruit is for.

Paul is writing to people who know the law, so Israel makes sense as a guess. But he says they belong to the risen Christ in order that we might bear fruit to God (Romans 7:4). The fruit isn't borne to a nation. It's borne to God.

You've got it, baker. Paul says the sinful passions were aroused by the law (Romans 7:5). That's a surprising thing to say, and he's going to spend the next verses explaining it. He's not blaming the law itself, and he'll say so plainly.

The world has plenty of blame in other places, friend, but not in this sentence. Paul says the sinful passions were aroused by the law (Romans 7:5). That's a strange thing to hear, and he stops to explain it soon after.

Peer pressure is a real thing, but Paul doesn't say it here. He says the sinful passions were aroused by the law (Romans 7:5). He doesn't mention a crowd anywhere in these verses. The word he uses is law, and he's about to clear up what he means.

Yes, baker. Paul says the sinful passions were at work in our bodies, "bearing fruit for death." (Romans 7:5) It's the opposite of the fruit he just mentioned in verse 4, the kind borne to God. Two kinds of fruit, and they end up in very different places.

This one is true, friend, and it's a heavy one. Paul says the sinful passions were at work in our bodies, "bearing fruit for death." (Romans 7:5) Right before that, he spoke of bearing fruit to God (Romans 7:4). Those two kinds of fruit head in opposite directions.

explanations.answer: In the new way of the Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says we have been released from the law so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit (Romans 7:6). The service doesn't stop. What changes is the way it's done. I know a bit about getting taken out of the dark and handed a new job, and it's a good feeling.

explanations.answer: In the old way of the written code
explanations.explanation: That's the one Paul says they're leaving behind, friend. They serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code (Romans 7:6). He puts the two side by side so the difference is clear. Released means the old way isn't the way anymore.

explanations.answer: In the strict way of the elders
explanations.explanation: Paul never brings up elders in this verse. He says they serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code (Romans 7:6). The contrast he draws is between the Spirit and the written code. That's the whole choice on the table.
Paul says the opposite, baker. He asks, "Is the law sin?" and answers, "Certainly not!" (Romans 7:7) He's heard how the last few verses sounded, and he stops to say it plainly. The law is not sin.

That's right, friend. Paul asks, "Is the law sin?" and answers, "Certainly not!" (Romans 7:7) You can almost hear him shutting that door before anyone walks through it. He's about to explain what the law actually does.

That's his example, baker. Paul says he would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet." (Romans 7:7) It's one sin he picks out of the list to make his point. The command named it, and then he knew.

Lying is a sin, but it's not the one Paul picks here. He says he would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet." (Romans 7:7) Coveting is his one example. That's the word he uses.

Stealing and coveting live pretty close together, friend, so I get the mix-up. But the sin Paul names is coveting. He says he would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, "Do not covet." (Romans 7:7)

Yes, baker. Paul says, "For apart from the law, sin is dead." (Romans 7:8) He's describing how sin used the commandment to produce every kind of covetous desire in him. Sin found its opening through the commandment.

It's in the text, friend. Paul says, "For apart from the law, sin is dead." (Romans 7:8) Just before that, he says sin seized its opportunity through the commandment and produced in him every kind of covetous desire. It's a heavy thing to say, so I think he wants us to slow down and read it twice.

Careful, baker, Paul says it the other way around. He calls it "…the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death." (Romans 7:10) The commandment was meant to bring life, and what he got was death. That surprise is what he's pointing at.

That's right. Paul says, "So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death." (Romans 7:10) Meant to bring life, and it brought death to him. I think that's why he says he discovered it, like it caught him off guard.

That's what Paul says, baker. Sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived him and through the commandment put him to death (Romans 7:11). Notice who does the deceiving. It's sin, not the commandment.
Nothing about this one came with a prize, friend. Paul says sin deceived him and through the commandment put him to death (Romans 7:11). No reward in that sentence. Sin deceived him.

If only sin had ignored him! Paul says the opposite: sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived him and put him to death (Romans 7:11). Sin was paying close attention. It used the opening it found.
Yes, baker. After everything he said, Paul concludes, "So then, the law is holy…" (Romans 7:12) He keeps blaming sin, and he never blames the law. He's not backing off from the law at all.
I can see why a person might reach for that after all that talk of death, friend. But Paul says the law is holy (Romans 7:12). Weak isn't his word for it. He puts the problem on sin.

After a passage this heavy, harsh feels like a fair guess. But Paul says, "So then, the law is holy…" (Romans 7:12). He goes on to call the commandment holy, righteous, and good. Harsh isn't a word he uses for either one.

explanations.answer: So sin would be exposed as sin
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Paul gives, baker. He says it was in order that sin might be exposed as sin (Romans 7:13). He also says that through the commandment, sin might become utterly sinful. Sin gets shown for what it is, and the good commandment is not the one to blame.

explanations.answer: So the law would look stronger
explanations.explanation: Paul never says the law needed a boost, friend. He gives this reason: in order that sin might be exposed as sin (Romans 7:13). The focus is on sin being shown for what it is, not on how the law looks.

explanations.answer: So Paul would learn to obey
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, baker, but it's not what Paul says. His reason is that sin might be exposed as sin (Romans 7:13). He adds that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful. He doesn't say it was about learning to obey.
